## **QUESTION 4 [50]**

It's no secret that colleges in the US have been preparing for an "enrollment cliff" as a result of declining birthrates, political factors over the ROI of college, etc.  Thus, enrollment is of peak interest. (For more information, check out this article from [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/davidrosowsky/2024/02/03/the-cliffs-of-higher-ed-whos-going-over-and-why/).)

Make sure the "us_district_enrollment_2016-2023.txt" file is in your working directory.  (Not sure about your working directory?  Run `getwd()` to find out where R is looking for the file.)  Then complete the following problems to dig further into enrollment trends.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4A [5]

Uncomment the code below.  Replace my working directory with your working directory in the `my_working_dir` variable.  Then run the entire code block below to read in the dataset.  Note: Make sure your working directory has a slash at the end of it.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
 my_working_dir="C:/Users/caden/Data_152/Datasets/"
 the_file="us_district_enrollment_2016-2023.txt"
# 
 full_path=paste(my_working_dir,the_file,sep="")
# 
 ds=read_csv(full_path, col_types = 'cfddddddd')

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4B [5]

Print the first 20 lines of the dataset using `head()`.

```{r}
head(ds)

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Use `names()` to print the names of the columns in the dataset.

```{r}

```


### 4E [5]

Let's customize the analysis. Filter `ds` to only include data for YOUR home state. (If your home state isn't US-based, you may pick a random state.)  Name this dataset `enroll`.

```{r}
enroll = ds %>% filter(State== "MONTANA")

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4F [5]

How many rows and columns are in `enroll`?

```{r}
view(enroll)
ncol(enroll)
nrow(enroll)
# 9 columns and 493 rows
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4G [5]

Which district had the highest enrollment in the 2022-2023 school year? Use `arrange` to answer this question.

```{r}
arrange(enroll,desc(`Total Students All Grades  2022-23`) )

```

**ANSWER:** Billings ELEM

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4H [5]

Uncomment and run the following code to reshape the `enroll` dataset. 

```{r}
 enroll2=enroll %>%
 	pivot_longer(
 		cols=`Total Students All Grades  2022-23`:`Total Students All Grades  2016-17`,
 		names_to="School_Year",
 		values_to="Enrollment"
 	) %>%
 	mutate(
 		School_Year=str_replace_all(
 			str_remove(School_Year,"Total Students All Grades  "),
 			"-","-20")
	)

 head(enroll2,15)
```


Using `enroll2`, create a summary table that shows the median district enrollment for each year represented in `enroll2`.  Hint: `group_by`, `summarize`

```{r}
med_enroll = enroll2 %>% group_by(District, School_Year)  %>% summarize(Median_Enrollment = median(Enrollment, na.rm = TRUE))


```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4I [10]

Create a graph of your choosing that showcases enrollment trends in your home state over time.  Make sure your graph is interpretable and clearly labeled.

```{r}
med_enroll %>% ggplot(aes(x = School_Year, y = Median_Enrollment, group = District, )) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = paste("Enrollment Trends in Montana"),
    x = "School Year",
    y = "Total Enrollment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
